title: network-path-architecture-notes
content:
Purpose:
Notes and working design for the Network Path Architecture that supports multi-region routing, strong mTLS, and policy-driven control plane decisions for Redwood Inference deployments. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: tradeoffs, incremental rollout, and measurable SLOs are emphasized.

Context & goals:
- We serve inference traffic across hosted, dedicated, and private modes; traffic can originate from external customers (hosted API), internal control-plane operations, and internal telemetry/observability pipelines.
- Constraints: low tail latency targets (p95 < 120ms for text gen happy paths), predictable failover between regions, regulatory requirement to keep some egress within customer VPCs (for Private customers), and minimizing extra GPU-bound token latency from network hops.
- Primary goals: secure ingress/egress with strong mutual auth, deterministic routing policies (latency/cost/tenant isolation), and an ops-friendly control plane for regional failover and canary rollouts.

High-level approach (one-liner):
Edge-terminated TLS for public API, regional Envoy ingress gateways with sidecar-enabled mTLS to compute planes, centralized control plane that pushes region-aware routing rules and model-variant fallbacks, and an egress-proxy pattern for outbound controls and auditability.

Ingress patterns (options and recommended path):
- Option A (recommended for hosted API): Cloud CDN/Edge LB terminates TLS (certs via ACM/Let's Encrypt), does initial WAF and rate-limit. Edge forwards to regional ingress tier (Envoy gateway or cloud LB) with mutual TLS between edge and region.
  - Rationale: reduces TLS handshake CPU on regional nodes, keeps certificate lifecycle simpler, allows edge to implement global DDoS/WAF.
  - Tradeoff: more trust at edge. Mitigation: mTLS between edge and regional gateways, signed JWT verification at ingress.
- Option B (private customers / VPC): TLS passthrough to customer-dedicated ingress (no termination at public edge). For Private on-prem, ingress lives in customer network and we use reverse-proxy connector to control plane.
- Recommendation: support both. Default hosted path: edge termination + mutual auth to regional ingress. Private path: passthrough or customer-managed termination.

Regional ingress tier design:
- Components: edge -> regional envoy gateway (ingress gateway) -> auth/token proxy -> local routing to model serving pools.
- Envoy provides L7 routing, healthchecks, circuit breaking and observability. Use TCP/TLS passthrough for low-latency model streams where possible (e.g., streaming WebSocket token streams).
- Keep path short: prefer 2 network hops (edge -> region gateway -> serving node) for best latency. Avoid extra layer of mesh for ingress if not necessary.

mTLS strategy and identity model:
- Use SPIFFE IDs for all service identities. Leverage a centralized identity authority (SPIRE or cloud equivalent) for issuing short-lived X.509 certs.
- Certificate lifecycle: certs rotated every 24h by default, with smooth hot-reload in Envoy and sidecars. Use SDS (secret discovery service) to push certs to proxies.
- Trust model: regional trust roots are derived from central root; control-plane distributes bundle. For Private customers with dedicated control plane, allow customer-managed root (bring-your-own-root).
- Sidecar vs gateway mTLS: prefer mTLS at sidecar only between platform control-plane + critical services. For high-throughput model-serving paths we recommend minimizing per-request TLS termination in-process; instead terminate at the local envoy and use local socket to model runtime (intra-node IPC) when on same host.

Service mesh considerations (lightweight vs full):
- Benefits of mesh: uniform mTLS, telemetry, consistent routing primitives (retries, timeouts, canary).
- Costs: CPU overhead for high-token-rate paths, increased tail latency, operational complexity for upgrades.
- Recommended approach: hybrid. Provide a lightweight sidecar baseline (Linkerd-like) for control-plane and orchestration paths, but run a stripped-down Envoy gateway for high-throughput inference nodes with explicit opt-in integration with mesh capabilities (e.g., traffic shaping, observability hooks).
- When to enable full mesh: tenant isolation experiments, A/B routing requiring fine-grained per-tenant control, or when using advanced L7 features that offset latency cost.

Routing policies and policy engine design:
- Inputs for routing decisions: origin (customer id, tier), region affinity, observed latency to regional pools, model version compatibility, cost/price tier, capacity signals, and configured customer constraints (e.g., data residency).
- Policy evaluation: keep evaluation at the ingress gateway (fast path) for per-request routing decisions, but manage complex policy rules in the control plane. Control plane compiles rules to simple match-action tables pushed to gateways.
- Examples:
  - Latency-aware: prefer local-region pool if p95_local < 1.2 * global_min_p95 and pool has available capacity.
  - Cost-aware fallback: if dedicated pool overloaded, route to cheaper quantized variant in another region, but only if customer allows cross-region inference.
  - Canary/rollout: control-plane tags X% traffic to new model variant within region using deterministic hashing on request id. Canary decisions are pushed as route percentages to gateways.

Control plane architecture for routing and policy distribution:
- Centralized control plane (global) holds canonical policy and topology, with a regional control-plane cache that serves local gateways. Communication: control plane -> regional caches -> gateways. Use streaming RPC (gRPC) with sequence numbers and delta updates to reduce churn.
- Consistency model: eventual with strong versioning for route tables. Gateways must be able to fallback to previous route table on mismatch.
- Safety: all control-plane changes pass through validated simulation (local traffic shadow) and safety checks (e.g., will-failover test). JIRA-PLT-782 covers the simulation harness.

Egress and outbound controls:
- Use a regional egress-proxy cluster that all outbound requests (to external APIs, telemetry sinks, model registries) pass through. This enables: egress ACLs, audit logging, and centralized NAT.
- For Private customers with VPC-restricted egress: support an egress connector that routes through customer-owned NAT or private peering.
- For telemetry and metrics: prefer ingest endpoints inside region to reduce cross-region egress costs; provide backlog-and-batch behavior under network degradation.

Performance and SLO considerations:
- Measure added RTT per hop: target < 6ms added by gateway hop inside region. If observed > 10ms, need to optimize or co-locate serving and gateway.
- CPU overhead budget: sidecars + envoys must not exceed 8-12% of node CPU capacity for inference nodes at steady state. If exceeded, consider kernel-bypass or user-space proxies and push more functionality into the fast path.

Failure modes and mitigations:
- Region outage: automatic routing to healthy regions using control plane policy. Must enforce data residency guardrails—if customer disallows cross-region, route to dedicated fallback in same geography or return 503 with clear error.
- Cert authority compromise or rotation outage: fallback to cached trusted bundles in gateway for grace period (configurable, e.g., 1h).
- Control-plane partition: regional caches must be capable of operating in read-only mode with cached policy. Provide manual operator overrides via CLI that write to local cache.

Security & compliance notes:
- Audit logging: ingress gateways and egress proxies must emit immutable audit events for per-request routing decisions (customer id, model variant, route chosen, region) to a compliant log store.
- Data residency: explicitly annotate routes with residency metadata; control plane rejects any route that violates customer constraints.
- Penetration testing: include gateway-to-serving path in pentest scope; attack surface includes edge LB, gateway, and sidecar identity endpoints.

Operational runbook highlights (short):
- Canary rollback: control-plane supports atomic route percentage rollback within 30s. Runbook step: set rollback percentage to 0, verify p95 stabilizes, escalate on metric drift.
- Certificate expiry: automated alert if any gateway reports cert TTL < 20m. Escalation path to SPIRE ops.
- Unexpected cross-region traffic spike: autoscale model pools and if not possible, trigger capacity-based routing to quantized variants or slow-path with clear 429/503 responses.

Open questions / tradeoffs to resolve (TODOs):
- How aggressive should cert rotation be for sidecars on inference nodes where process restarts are disruptive? Possible: 24h certs with staggered rollouts vs 7d for serving nodes. (Owner: Jonah)
- Which mesh tech to standardize on for control-plane services? Linkerd is lower overhead; Istio has richer policy primitives. (Owner: Priya)
- Quantization routing policy: should cost-based fallback be automatic for all hosted customers or opt-in per tenant? (Owner: Marek)

Immediate next steps and action items:
- Build a small regional prototype (eu-west) with edge -> envoy gateway -> single serving pool. Measure added RTT and CPU overhead. (Owner: Asha, due 2026-03-20)
- Draft confluence page for policy language and route compilation format (spec needed for gateway implementers). (Owner: Priya, due 2026-03-15)
- Create JIRA epic for identity lifecycle and SPIRE integration (JIRA-PLT-790). (Owner: Jonah, due 2026-03-10)

Notes to self / working comments: 
- Keep fast-path as small as possible; more complex features should be opt-in.
- Collect real-world p95/p99 from current hosted cluster to baseline impact of adding a gateway hop.
- Consider kernel tuning (SO_REUSEPORT, eBPF accept-side steering) for high-connection-rate scenarios.
